title: Normal Distributions
p: In the last section, we learned how to calculate probabilities based on standard normal distributions for any z-score. We also learned how to calculate these probablities as area under the curve in the left-tail of the distribution, the right-tail of the distribution, or between two z-scores.
In this lesson, we will learn how to compute normal distribution probabilities for bell-shaped data that has any mean or standard devation.

section.title: Z-Scores

example.title: Example 1
example.p: Suppose a data set has a mean of 12.4 and a standard deviation of 2.3. Calculate a z-score for the value x=17.6. Round your answer to two decimal places.

section.p:
You can tell if a value is larger or smaller than the mean by checking if its z-score is positive or negative. This is because the standard deviation of a data set is always a postive value, so whether a z-score is positive or negative is dependent entirely on the value of: x-\mu. Therefore, if:
z > 0, then the value x is larger than the mean
z < 0, then the value x is smaller than the mean
z = 0, then the value x is equal to the mean

example.title: Example 2
example.p:
A data value within a data set has a z-score of z=-1.35. Is the value:
Larger than the mean Smaller than the mean It is impossible to tell

section.p: The importance of z-scores becomes apparent when we realize that they have the ability to convert a data set into a new data set that has a mean of zero, and standard deviation of one, all while preserving the shape of the original distribution. Let's explore this through an example.

section.title: Calculating Normal Distribution Probabilities
section.p: Z-scores are important because they give us a way to work with any normal distribution using the standard normal distribution.

The standard normal distribution is a bell-shaped distribution with a mean of zero and a standard deviation of one. Z-scores allow us to transform values from any normal distribution into values on this standard scale, while keeping the same relative position within the distribution. This means that we can use the standard normal distribution to find probabilities for any normal distribution.
The good news is that we don’t need to convert an entire data set into z-scores. We only need to convert the values that are important for solving the problem.

Watch the following video animation (no audio) to see how a normal distribution with any mean and standard deviation can be transformed into the standard normal distribution. Notice that the area to the left of a particular x-value stays the same when we convert that value to its corresponding z-score.

section:
Use of Technology
It is common for many types of technology to calculate z-scores for you during the process of finding normal distribution probabilities. This is convenient, and can even help eleviate rounding errors, but you should understand how to use z-scores first before taking advantage of these conveniences.

problem.p: The length of time it takes a student to complete a particular math exam is normally distributed with a mean of 40 minutes and a standard deviation of 5.2 minutes. If a class period has 50 minutes for the exam, what is the probability that a student selected at random will have time to complete it, and finish in less than 50 minutes?

problem.feedback: If the student finishes the exam in more than 50 minutes, then the class period will be over, so this can't be a right-tail probability.

You could solve this problem by calculating the probability that a student finishes between 0 and 50 minutes, but imposing a boundary that doesn't already exist in the problem (the lower bound of zero minutes) can lead you to incorrect values sometimes in Statistics. It is better to avoid this practice.
